en: Saṁyutta Nikāya 28.1 (SN 28.1, PTS SN iii 235) 1. Sāriputta-vagga Vivekaja-sutta (Born of Seclusion) At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, there are these four jhānas. What four? Here, bhikkhus, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. This is called the first jhāna. “Again, with the subsiding of thought and examination, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration. This is called the second jhāna. “Again, with the fading away as well of rapture, a bhikkhu dwells equanimous and, mindful and clearly comprehending, he experiences happiness with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: ‘He is equanimous, mindful, one who dwells happily. This is called the third jhāna. “Again, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. This is called the fourth jhāna. “These, bhikkhus, are the four jhānas.”
On one occasion the Venerable Sāriputta was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Sāriputta dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Sāvatthī for alms.
Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī, after his meal, returning from his almsround, he went to the Blind Men’s Grove for his midday rest.
Having plunged into the Andhavana forest, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree for his midday rest.
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Sāriputta emerged from seclusion and approached Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
The Venerable Ānanda saw the Venerable Sāriputta coming from afar.
Having seen him, he said this to the Venerable Sāriputta:
"Friend Sāriputta, your faculties are serene; the color of your face is pure and bright.
By what dwelling did the Venerable Sāriputta dwell today?"

“Here, friends, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I enter and dwell in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.
Regarding this, friends, it does not occur to me:
‘I am entering the first jhāna,’ or ‘I have entered the first jhāna,’ or ‘I have emerged from the first jhāna.’”
For indeed, in the Venerable Sāriputta, the underlying tendencies of the conceits of "I-making," "mine-making," and the "conceit 'I am'" have been thoroughly uprooted for a long time.
Therefore, it does not occur to the Venerable Sāriputta:
"I am attaining the first jhāna," or "I have attained the first jhāna," or "I have emerged from the first jhāna."
First.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 28.2 (SN 28.2, PTS SN iii 235) 1.
Sāriputta-vagga
The Discourse on the Absence of Applied Thought. The setting was at Sāvatthī.
The Venerable Ānanda saw [the Venerable Sāriputta]... [and] said this to the Venerable Sāriputta:
“Friend Sāriputta, your faculties are serene; the color of your face is pure and bright.
By means of what dwelling did the Venerable Sāriputta dwell today?

“Here, friend, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, I entered and dwelt in the second jhāna, which is internal tranquility and singleness of mind, free from applied and sustained thought, born of concentration, and filled with rapture and happiness.”
"Friends, it does not occur to me:
'I am entering the second jhāna,' or 'I have entered the second jhāna,' or 'I have emerged from the second jhāna.
This is because for the Venerable Sāriputta, the underlying tendencies of I-making, mine-making, and the conceit 'I am' have been thoroughly uprooted for a long time."
Therefore, it does not occur to the Venerable Sāriputta:
"I am entering the second jhāna," or "I have entered the second jhāna," or "I have emerged from the second jhāna. This is the second [section].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 28.3 (SN 28.3, PTS SN iii 236) 1. Sāriputta-vagga Pīti-sutta (The Discourse on Rapture) At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, when rapture arises in a bhikkhu, it is to be expected that his body will be tranquil, his mind will be tranquil, and he will dwell in comfort. When a bhikkhu’s body is tranquil and his mind is tranquil, he attains the cessation of perception and feeling. This is called a bhikkhu who has reached the ultimate conclusion in this very life.”
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
The Venerable Ānanda saw him...
[and said]: "Friend Sāriputta, your faculties are serene; the color of your face is pure and bright."
“In what dwelling did the Venerable Sāriputta dwell today?
“Here, friend, with the fading away of rapture, I dwelt equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, experiencing happiness with the body;
of which the Noble Ones declare: ‘He dwells happily, mindful and equanimous’—thus I dwelt in the third [jhāna].”
“I enter and dwell in the third jhāna.
Regarding this, friend, it does not occur to me:
‘I am attaining the third jhāna,’ or ‘I have attained the third jhāna,’ or ‘I have emerged from the third jhāna.’”
For indeed, for the venerable Sāriputta, the underlying tendencies of the conceits of "I-making," "mine-making," and the "conceit 'I am'" have been thoroughly uprooted for a long time.
Therefore, it does not occur to the venerable Sāriputta:
"I am attaining the third jhāna," or "I have attained the third jhāna," or "I have emerged from the third jhāna."
Third.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 28.4 (SN 28.4, PTS SN iii 237) 1.
Sāriputta-vagga (The Chapter on Sāriputta)
The Discourse on Equanimity.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
The Venerable Ānanda saw [the Blessed One]... [as before].
“Friend Sāriputta, your faculties are serene; your facial complexion is pure and bright.
By means of what dwelling did the Venerable Sāriputta dwell today?

“Here, friend, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, I entered and dwelt in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.”
"Friends, it does not occur to me:
'I am entering the fourth jhāna,' or 'I have entered the fourth jhāna,' or 'I have emerged from the fourth jhāna.
For indeed, for the Venerable Sāriputta, the underlying tendencies of I-making, mine-making, and the conceit 'I am' have been thoroughly uprooted for a long time."
Therefore, it does not occur to the Venerable Sāriputta:
"I am attaining the fourth jhāna," or "I have attained the fourth jhāna," or "I have emerged from the fourth jhāna.
This is the fourth.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 28.5 (SN 28.5, PTS SN iii 237) 1. Sāriputtavagga The Discourse on the Base of Infinite Space At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, just as when the ocean is deep, immeasurable, unfathomable, so too, bhikkhus, the base of infinite space is deep, immeasurable, unfathomable. It is impossible to fathom the base of infinite space with the mind, or with a mental standard, except by the abandoning of whatever is associated with form. “Just as when the sky is deep, immeasurable, unfathomable, so too, bhikkhus, the base of infinite space is deep, immeasurable, unfathomable. It is impossible to fathom the base of infinite space with the mind, or with a mental standard, except by the abandoning of whatever is associated with form.”
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
The Venerable Ānanda saw [the Blessed One]... [He said:

"In this case, friend, by completely transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking 'space is infinite,' I enter and dwell in the base of infinite space... [and so on].
“Or, ‘He has emerged’”—
the fifth [sutta].
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 28.6 (SN 28.6, PTS SN iii 237).
1. The Chapter on Sāriputta.
The Discourse on the Base of Infinite Consciousness.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
The Venerable Ānanda saw him... [and asked:
"In this case, friend, having completely transcended the base of infinite space, perceiving 'consciousness is infinite,' I enter and dwell in the base of infinite consciousness... [and so on]...
or have I emerged from it?"
The Sixth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 28.7 (SN 28.7, PTS SN iii 237) 1.
Sāriputtavagga (The Chapter with Sāriputta)

The Discourse on the Base of Nothingness. The setting was at Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Sāriputta …pe… [approached the Blessed One] … [and said: “Bhante, it is wonderful, Bhante; it is marvelous, Bhante, how well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘When, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is liberated in mind through the base of nothingness, he is called one who has reached the ultimate end, one who has attained the ultimate security from bondage, one who has arrived at the ultimate goal, one who has accomplished the ultimate holy life. “Sāriputta, when a bhikkhu is liberated in mind through the base of nothingness, he is indeed called one who has reached the ultimate end, one who has attained the ultimate security from bondage, one who has arrived at the ultimate goal, one who has accomplished the ultimate holy life. [The Venerable Sāriputta then asked: “But, Bhante, how is it that a bhikkhu is liberated in mind through the base of nothingness? “Here, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu, having completely transcended the base of infinite space, aware that ‘there is nothing,’ enters and dwells in the base of nothingness. It is in this way, Sāriputta, that a bhikkhu is liberated in mind through the base of nothingness. [The Venerable Sāriputta then asked: “But, Bhante, how does a bhikkhu, being liberated in mind through the base of nothingness, reach the ultimate end, attain the ultimate security from bondage, arrive at the ultimate goal, and accomplish the ultimate holy life? “Here, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu, having completely transcended the base of nothingness, enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Having completely transcended the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling. And, having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed. It is in this way, Sāriputta, that a bhikkhu, being liberated in mind through the base of nothingness, reaches the ultimate end, attains the ultimate security from bondage, arrives at the ultimate goal, and accomplishes the ultimate holy life. [The Venerable Sāriputta then said: “It is wonderful, Bhante; it is marvelous, Bhante, how well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘When, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is liberated in mind through the base of nothingness, he is called one who has reached the ultimate end, one who has attained the ultimate security from bondage, one who has arrived at the ultimate goal, one who has accomplished the ultimate holy life. [The Blessed One then said: “Sāriputta, when a bhikkhu is liberated in mind through the base of nothingness, he is indeed called one who has reached the ultimate end, one who has attained the ultimate security from bondage, one who has arrived at the ultimate goal, one who has accomplished the ultimate holy life. It is in this way, Sāriputta, that a bhikkhu is liberated in mind through the base of nothingness. Having completely transcended the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling. [The Venerable Sāriputta then said: “It is wonderful, Bhante; it is marvelous, Bhante, how well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘When, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is liberated in mind through the base of nothingness, he is called one who has reached the ultimate end, one who has attained the ultimate security from bondage, one who has arrived at the ultimate goal, one who has accomplished the ultimate holy life. “Here, friends, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, [perceiving] ‘there is nothing,’ I enter and dwell in the base of nothingness… ‘I have emerged’—
thus it is. This is the seventh.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 28.8 The Discourse on the Base of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception Sāriputta Chapter 1 At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Listen to that and attend closely; I will speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, here a bhikkhu, with the complete transcending of the base of nothingness, enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This is called the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. “Bhikkhus, I say that this base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is to be realized by direct knowledge, not by another’s word, not by hearsay, not by reasoned reflection, not by approval of a view, but by the destruction of the taints in one who has developed and cultivated it. “This, bhikkhus, is called the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. And this base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is to be realized by direct knowledge, not by another’s word, not by hearsay, not by reasoned reflection, not by approval of a view, but by the destruction of the taints in one who has developed and cultivated it.”
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta … [as before] … “In this case,
friend, by completely surmounting the base of nothingness, I enter and dwell in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception …” [as before].
“Or, ‘he has emerged’”—
the eighth [sutta].
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 28.9 (SN 28.9, PTS SN iii 238).
1. The Chapter on Sāriputta:
The Discourse on the Attainment of Cessation.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta… [as before] … “In this case,
friend, by completely transcending the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, I enter and dwell in the cessation of perception and feeling.
Regarding that, friend, it does not occur to me:”
“I am attaining the cessation of perception and feeling,” or “I have attained the cessation of perception and feeling,” or “I have emerged from the cessation of perception and feeling.
For indeed, for the Venerable Sāriputta, the underlying tendencies of I-making, mine-making, and the conceit “I am” have been thoroughly uprooted for a long time.
Therefore, it does not occur to the Venerable Sāriputta in this way:
“‘I am attaining the cessation of perception and feeling,’ or ‘I have attained the cessation of perception and feeling,’ or ‘I have emerged from the cessation of perception and feeling.
(The ninth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 28.10 (SN 28.10, PTS SN iii 238)
1. Sāriputta Chapter.
The Discourse on Sucimukhī.
At one time the Venerable Sāriputta was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Sāriputta dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagaha for alms.
Having walked for alms in Rājagaha from house to house, he sat down to eat that almsfood leaning against the base of a certain wall.
Then the female wanderer Sucimukhī approached the Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, she said this to the Venerable Sāriputta:
“Why, ascetic, do you eat with your face turned downwards?
“I do not eat with my face turned downwards, sister.
“In that case, ascetic, do you eat with your face turned upwards?”
“I do not eat facing upwards, sister.
“In that case, ascetic, you eat facing the directions?
“I do not eat facing the directions, sister.”
“In that case, ascetic, do you eat facing the intermediate directions?
“I do not, sister, eat facing the intermediate directions.
“When asked, ‘Ascetic, do you eat facing downwards? you replied, ‘I do not, sister, eat facing downwards.’”
“Then, ascetic, when you were asked, ‘Are you eating with your face turned upward? you replied, ‘No, sister, I am not eating with my face turned upward.
When you were asked, ‘Then, ascetic, are you eating with your face turned toward the cardinal directions? you replied, ‘No, sister, I am not eating with my face turned toward the cardinal directions.

When you were asked, ‘Then, ascetic, are you eating with your face turned toward the intermediate directions? you replied, ‘No, sister, I am not eating with my face turned toward the intermediate directions.’”
“But how, ascetic, do you eat?

“Sister, those ascetics and brahmins who make their living by the wrong livelihood of the science of omens and the science of animal cries—they, sister, are called ‘ascetics and brahmins who eat with their faces turned downwards.

Those ascetics and brahmins, sister, who make their living by the wrong livelihood of the science of astrology and the science of animal cries—they, sister, are called ‘ascetics and brahmins who eat with their faces turned upwards.’”

“Sister, whatever ascetics or brahmins make their living by means of wrong livelihood through the practice of acting as messengers or envoys, these, sister, are called ‘ascetics and brahmins who eat facing the cardinal directions.

Whatever ascetics or brahmins, sister, make their living by means of wrong livelihood through the science of bodily marks or the science of low arts, these, sister, are called ‘ascetics and brahmins who eat facing the intermediate directions.
But I, sister, do not make my living by means of wrong livelihood through the science of sites or the science of low arts.”
I do not maintain my life by wrong livelihood through the science of astrology or the low arts of divination;

I do not maintain my life by wrong livelihood through the practice of acting as a messenger or an envoy; I do not maintain my life by wrong livelihood through the science of bodily marks or the low arts of divination.
I seek almsfood in accordance with the Dhamma.
“Having sought almsfood in accordance with the Dhamma, I eat it.
Then the female wanderer Sucimukhī, going from street to street and from crossroads to crossroads in Rājagaha, proclaimed:
“The recluses, sons of the Sakyans, consume their food righteously;”
“The Sakyan monastics consume food that is blameless.
Give almsfood to the Sakyan monastics.
Tenth.
The first section, the Sāriputta-vagga.
Its summary verse:
Born of seclusion, without applied thought...
Joy and equanimity are the fourth;
space, consciousness, nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Cessation is said to be the ninth,
and the tenth is the Needle-Mouthed One.
The Saṃyutta on Sāriputta is complete.
